sentences: Professional sports have never generated as much money as they do today.
The best players earn huge sums, and the major clubs are increasingly resembling real businesses.
This evolution has positive aspects.
Thanks to this money, competitions are better organized, the stadiums are more modern, and the spectacle is more impressive.

When money dominates, passion sometimes takes a back seat.

sentences: For a long time, I brought back objects from my travels.
Small statues, decorated boxes, fridge magnets.
Almost all of them ended up in a drawer, and I would be unable to say which country half of them comes from.
What has remained, however, are things I hadn't planned to bring back.
Habits, first.
Since a stay in Spain, I have dinner later and I walk after the meal.
Since a trip to Japan, I take off my shoes when I enter my home, and I now find it strange to do otherwise.
These gestures entered my life without me deciding them.
Tastes, next.
I discovered a spice mix in a Moroccan market that I had never used.
I still buy it today, six years later, in a grocery store in my neighborhood.
And above all, a way of seeing.
It's harder to explain.
Living a few days in a place where the obvious things are not the same — the schedules, the role of family, the way of talking in the street — has a lasting effect.
You come back finding your own habits a little less natural.
This might be the true benefit of travel: not what you have seen, but what you stop considering as obvious.
Today, I hardly buy souvenirs anymore.
On the other hand, I write a few lines every evening.
This notebook is the only object I bring back, and it's the only one I reopen.

sentences: The French meal — an appetizer, a main course, cheese, and a dessert, enjoyed together and without rushing — has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage since 2010.
This recognition surprised some: can a way of eating really be classified?
The argument was, however, precise.
What was distinguished was not French cuisine, but the ritual: the set table, the order of the dishes, the act of eating together, and talking about what one is eating.
Has this ritual disappeared?
The numbers tell a nuanced story.
On one hand, it has clearly shortened.
The weekday lunch now lasts about thirty minutes on average, compared to much longer forty years ago.
Many employees eat in front of a screen, and sandwiches have taken on a considerable role.
The number of dishes has also decreased: few families serve four courses during the week.
On the other hand, something resists with real strength.
Compared to its neighbors, France maintains remarkably synchronized meal times: at one o'clock, a large part of the country eats at the same moment.
The meal remains predominantly a collective practice, seated and at the table.
And on weekends, the long meal reappears, especially on Sundays.
What has changed is not so much the value placed on the meal, but the space that work allows it during the week.
It would be excessive to talk about disappearance.
It is more accurate to say that the meal has become more concentrated: less frequent, but still important when it occurs.

sentences: It is estimated that several million French homes are considered to be "thermal sieves": poorly insulated, expensive to heat, uncomfortable in winter, and increasingly unbearable in summer.
The topic seems technical.
In reality, it is as much a social issue as an ecological one.
Heating accounts for a significant share of emissions related to housing, and buildings are one of the main sources of emissions in the country.
Reducing heating needs is therefore a major lever.
But the most immediate effect concerns the residents themselves.
Living in a poorly insulated home means paying more to be less well heated.
It is often the most modest households that occupy these homes, especially in rental situations.
This is referred to as "energy poverty": having to choose between heating properly and other essential expenses.
Why is renovation progressing slowly?
First, because it is expensive: a complete renovation costs tens of thousands of euros.
There are aids available, but the applications are complex and you often have to pay upfront.
Then, because the owner is not always the one who pays for heating.
A landlord has no direct financial incentive to insulate a property for which they do not pay the bills.
Finally, because the work is extensive and the number of trained craftsmen remains insufficient.
Measures have been taken, including the gradual ban on renting the least efficient homes.
These measures raise legitimate debates: if poorly implemented, they can reduce the rental supply.
But leaving millions of households in homes that are expensive to heat is not a viable policy either.

sentences: If we relied solely on the news, we would conclude that everything is getting worse, everywhere, all the time.

However, some long-term trends are moving in the opposite direction: global infant mortality has significantly decreased over a few decades, access to education has improved, and extreme poverty has declined.
This does not mean that everything is fine — inequalities, the climate, and several conflicts contradict any naive optimism.
But there is a clear gap between the image presented by the news and measurable trends.
This gap can be explained by the very nature of information.
A news item is, by definition, an event.
However, disasters are events, while progress is a process.
An earthquake occurs on a Tuesday; the gradual decrease in infant mortality does not happen on any particular day, so it is almost never reported.
There is also a well-documented psychological phenomenon: we give more weight to negative information than to positive.
Newsrooms did not invent this bias; they respond to it because we click more.
The result is a form of weariness.
Many people say they avoid the news — not out of disinterest, but out of fatigue.
What to do?
Completely cutting off is not satisfying: staying informed is part of collective life.
What works for many comes down to two adjustments.
Choosing defined moments rather than a continuous flow, which increases anxiety without enhancing understanding.
And favoring long formats that explain trends, rather than the accumulation of alerts.
Being informed is not about knowing everything in real time.
It is about understanding what is happening.

sentences: Feeding birds in winter is a very common and generally beneficial practice.
It helps many species survive the period when natural food is scarce, and it allows many people to observe wildlife up close.
However, it requires some precautions, which conservation organizations regularly remind us of.
The first one concerns the timing.
Feeding is useful from the end of autumn to the end of winter, as long as the cold persists.
On the other hand, it is not recommended in spring and summer: chicks need protein-rich insects, and seeds provided at that time can be harmful to them.
The second precaution concerns the food.
Unsalted sunflower seeds and fat balls are suitable for many species.
Bread, on the other hand, should be avoided: it swells, provides poor nutrition, and can cause digestive issues.
Any salty food should be avoided.
The third precaution is the most important and the most often forgotten: hygiene.
A feeder concentrates dozens of birds in one place, which facilitates the transmission of diseases.
Epidemics affecting certain species have been documented and partly attributed to poorly maintained feeders.
Therefore, it is important to regularly clean the feeder, remove damp leftovers, and occasionally move the feeding spot.
One last piece of advice is worth mentioning: once you start, it's better to continue until the end of winter.
Birds incorporate the resource into their daily movements.
And if you really want to help, the best action is not the feeder.
It's to plant a hedge.

sentences: “Speak English fluently in thirty days.” “The secret method that schools are hiding from you.” Promises like these are everywhere, and they sell well because they meet a real desire: to learn quickly and effortlessly.
However, they are based on a lie, or at least on a carefully maintained inaccuracy.
The first problem is the word 'fluently.'
It doesn't have a clear definition.
Ordering a coffee and debating philosophy are two levels separated by years.
A method can make you able to say a few sentences in a month — that's true — and then call that 'fluently.'
The second problem is the erasure of real time.
All serious estimates converge: reaching a conversational level in a language requires hundreds of hours of practice.
No method eliminates these hours.
Some make them more effective or more enjoyable, which is already valuable, but none replace them.
That doesn't mean that all methods are equal.
Real differences exist.
Approaches that encourage speaking early, expose you to real language, and rely on spaced repetition work better than memorizing lists or abstract grammar.
But the best method remains, by far, the one that you actually use.
A perfect app abandoned after two weeks is worth less than a mediocre method practiced for a year.
The real secret, if there is one, is disappointingly banal.
A little, every day, for a long time, with real contact with the language.
It's not marketable.
It's simply what works.

sentences: Among all the rituals that once structured daily life, the shared meal is one of the last to endure.
Meeting at a fixed time, around the same table, to eat together: this seemingly mundane gesture is also one of the few moments when a family or community truly comes together.
However, this ritual, long taken for granted, is gradually unraveling, and it's worth considering what is at stake in this slow dissolution.
The causes are well known.
Schedules have become desynchronized: everyone eats when they can, according to their timetable.
Screens have made their way to the table, capturing the gazes that once met.
Individual food, eaten alone and in haste, has gained ground over shared dishes.
Little by little, the meal is ceasing to be a moment of gathering and is becoming a simple function, carried out by each person on their own.
What is being lost in this evolution is not insignificant.
The shared meal is not just about food; it is a space for conversation, transmission, and connection.
It is often here that news is exchanged, where children learn to listen and speak, and where, day after day, the invisible threads that connect family members are woven.
Eliminate this moment, and you do not just remove a dinner: you take away one of the main supports of communal life.
Studies on the subject confirm this intuition.
Where meals are regularly shared, family bonds are stronger, and children themselves benefit in many ways.

Not that the meal has magical virtues, but because it creates what modern life offers increasingly rarely: a regular, predictable time where we are simply together, with no other purpose than to be there.
Preserving this ritual does not require great means, just a decision: to treat the shared meal as an important appointment, and not as a variable adjustment.
Turning off screens, waiting for one another, making dinner a protected moment: these modest choices are often enough to save what, once lost, is hard to regain.
In a world that scatters our lives, the shared meal remains one of the last places where we can gather every day.
It would be a strange poverty to let it disappear through simple neglect.

sentences: In the face of climate change, a question often arises, often tinged with discouragement: what's the point?
What weight can my gesture, so modest, have in the face of such a vast problem?
I sort my waste, I reduce my consumption, while entire industries continue to pollute massively.
Isn't it ridiculous, even hypocritical?
This question is legitimate, and it deserves an honest answer that neither resorts to guilt nor offers empty reassurances.
We must first acknowledge a grain of truth in the doubt.
Yes, on a planetary scale, an individual's gesture is tiny.
No, sorting our waste alone will not be enough to solve the climate crisis.

Those who let others believe that responsibility rests entirely on consumers are making a mistake, and sometimes an act of dishonesty: they divert attention from the collective and industrial decisions that truly weigh heavily.
But drawing the conclusion from this observation that our gestures are useless would be another error, symmetrical and just as convenient.
For this conclusion, in reality, is quite convenient: it provides a perfect excuse to change nothing.
"Since it’s useless, we might as well continue as before." The feeling of powerlessness then becomes a comfortable justification for inaction.
However, our gestures matter for several reasons.
First, because when added together, the behaviors of millions of people actually begin to weigh.
Then, because our individual actions are not isolated: they influence those around us, shape norms, and make some changes desirable while rendering others shameful.
Someone who changes their way of living does not only change their own impact; they slightly shift what seems normal.
Finally, and perhaps most importantly, there is a link between our actions and our beliefs.
It's difficult to demand deep changes while refusing to make any oneself.
Our gestures, even modest ones, commit us, lend credibility to our demands, and transform us into coherent citizens rather than powerless spectators.
The real answer is therefore not to choose between individual action and collective action, as if one excludes the other.
It is to understand that they mutually nourish each other.
Changing one’s life without ever influencing collective decisions would be insufficient; demanding collective changes without ever changing anything in one’s life would be lacking in credibility.
The two go hand in hand, and it is their conjunction that alone can hope to make a difference.
We live surrounded by images of bodies.
On screens, in advertising, on social media, idealized silhouettes constantly parade: slim, firm, young, and flawless.
This flood of images, historically unprecedented in its scale, does not fail to affect how each person perceives their own body.
And this effect, studies confirm, is most often negative.
The mechanism is that of comparison.
By constantly seeing idealized bodies, we take these images as the norm, and our own body, judged by this standard, always seems insufficient.
What we compare, however, is not comparable: the images around us are selected, retouched, staged, while our body appears to us in its ordinary reality.
We measure ourselves against a perfection that does not exist, and we inevitably find ourselves lacking.
This constant comparison has a real cost.
Dissatisfaction, shame, obsession with control, and sometimes serious eating disorders: bodily distress, particularly widespread among the young, is far from trivial.
It is not a mere vanity, but a suffering that can invade one's entire life, robbing those who experience it of a part of their self-esteem.
We must also recognize how arbitrary and changeable these norms are.
What is presented today as the ideal body is not universal: other eras and cultures have valued entirely different silhouettes.
The current ideal is not a truth of nature, but a social construct, shaped notably by commercial interests.
For we must not forget: a significant part of this dissatisfaction is deliberately maintained because it drives sales.
Recognizing this is not enough to free oneself from it, but it helps to gain perspective.
Understanding that these images are manipulated, that these norms are arbitrary, and that this distress is partly manufactured is the beginning of loosening their grip.
We can also choose what we look at, turn away from sources that fuel comparison, and seek more diverse and authentic representations of real bodies.
The body is not primarily an object to be displayed, a product to conform to a norm.
It is what we live through, experience, and act with.
Reconnecting with this truth — inhabiting one's body rather than judging it — may be the first step towards a peace that no perfect image will ever provide.

sentences: "There’s no arguing about tastes and colors," says popular wisdom.
Everyone has their own preferences, which are equally valid, and it would be futile — even pretentious — to judge the tastes of others.
This idea, which seems to promote tolerance, deserves to be questioned.
For while it contains a grain of truth, it also hides a more disturbing one: is everything really equal when it comes to taste?
First, let’s acknowledge what this saying gets right.
Our tastes are partly irreducibly personal, shaped by our history, our sensitivity, and our memories.
No one can prove to me that I should like one piece of music over another, and it’s absurd to try to impose one’s preferences as truths.
In this sense, tastes are not up for debate: they are experienced, and no one has the right to dictate to another what they should feel.
But to stop there would be too simple.
For if all tastes were strictly equivalent, some consequences would be hard to accept.
Should we say that a profound work and a crude production are equal, just because each has its fans?
That the judgment of a connoisseur, who has long engaged with an art, is no more valuable than that of an ignorant person?
The idea that "everything is equal" leads to these conclusions, which clash with our experience.
There is a difference between taste as mere preference and taste as discernment.
The former is purely subjective: I like it or I don’t, and that’s not up for discussion.
The latter is cultivated, refined, and educated: as one engages with an art, one learns to perceive nuances, qualities, and depths that were not initially visible.
This kind of taste is not arbitrary; it rests on acquired familiarity, and for that reason, it can be discussed, argued about, and transmitted.
Recognizing this is not elitist, provided one does not confuse discernment with disdain.
Saying that some judgments are more enlightened than others does not mean looking down on those who enjoy simple things; it merely asserts that taste can deepen, and that it’s worth cultivating.
Someone who has learned to appreciate complex music does not have a "better" taste as a person; they have a more developed taste, which opens up richer pleasures.
In summary, taste can both be discussed and not discussed, depending on what one means by that.
As raw preference, it escapes discussion; as cultivated discernment, it invites it.
Between the relativism that levels everything and the arrogance that scorns, there is room for a more just attitude: to respect everyone’s tastes while believing it’s worth educating one’s own.

sentences: The world is complicated.
The phenomena around us — social, economic, natural — often result from multiple, intertwined causes that are difficult to untangle.
However, our mind, faced with this complexity, feels uneasy and instinctively seeks to dispel it.
It prefers simple, clear explanations that reassure and are easy to remember.
This preference, quite natural, is also one of our most dangerous weaknesses, because what is simple to understand is not necessarily true.
The temptation of simple explanations takes recognizable forms.
It seeks a single cause where there are several: this problem comes from one thing, and one thing only.
It designates a convenient scapegoat: if things go wrong, it's the fault of a certain group, a certain decision, a certain person.
It reduces a complex reality to a stark opposition, to a clear narrative where good and evil, cause and effect, can be identified effortlessly.
These explanations have immense appeal: they soothe the discomfort of uncertainty and give the feeling of understanding.
This appeal explains the success of theories that claim to explain everything by a single hidden cause.
Faced with troubling events, whose real causes are diffuse and disappointing, the mind is seduced by the idea that a plan, a will, a culprit might be hiding behind everything.
Such explanations have clarity and drama on their side; they transform the bewildering disorder of reality into a satisfying narrative.
That they are false does not prevent them from being believed, because they respond to a need stronger than the concern for truth: the need to understand, or to believe we understand.
Resisting this temptation requires effort, and even a certain courage: the courage to accept complexity, to tolerate uncertainty, to acknowledge that we do not understand everything.
It is more comfortable to hold a simple and false explanation than to admit that the truth is complicated, uncertain, and perhaps partly out of reach.
Accepting not to take sides, to suspend judgment, to live with questions that have no clear answers, goes against our most natural inclination.
Yet it is at this price that we escape reassuring illusions.
This does not mean we should retreat into a paralyzing skepticism, where nothing would ever be explainable.
Not all explanations are equal, and some, although complex, are well established.
It is not about giving up understanding, but about being wary of overly easy understandings, preferring a complicated truth to a clear lie.
Simplicity can be a mark of deep thought; it is more often a sign of lazy thinking.

To challenge simple explanations is to cultivate a form of intellectual maturity: one that prefers the discomfort of the true to the comfort of the false, which accepts that the world resists our desires for clarity.
In a time when so many voices offer clear answers to complex questions, this skepticism is not a luxury; it is a necessity.

sentences: We are the being that knows it will die.
This awareness, which we may share with no one else, is one of the strangest and heaviest aspects of the human condition.
We live knowing that we will die, that everything we do, love, and build will come to an end.
One might think that this awareness is merely a source of anxiety, a burden from which it would be better to turn away.
But it is also, when properly considered, what can give life its depth and value.
This final text of a whole journey deserves to be reflected upon.
The most common temptation is to flee from this awareness, to live as if we do not have to die.
Our time excels in this avoidance: it hides death, pushes it out of sight, surrounds it with silence, and constantly distracts us so we do not think about it.
This flight is understandable — the thought of death is difficult — but it comes at a price.
By refusing to confront our finitude, we often live in a kind of illusion, as if we had infinite time, postponing what is essential, wasting days we believe are countless.
The forgetting of death fosters a certain unconsciousness of life.
For, paradoxically, it is the awareness of death that can give life all its value.
If we lived forever, nothing would be urgent, nothing would be pressing, each moment could be postponed indefinitely; time, unlimited, would lose its value.
It is because our days are numbered that they are precious, that each moment is unique and will not return, that our choices carry weight.
Finitude, far from making life absurd, may be what makes it intense.
What is rare and finite has value; what is infinite and unlimited no longer does.
The awareness of death, when well received, is thus a teacher of life.
It reminds us of what truly matters, distinguishes the essential from the trivial, and frees us from the vanities that consume us.
In the face of the thought of our end, we stop fretting over trivialities, we measure the value of loved ones, of the present time, of simple things.
Many wisdoms have made meditation on death not a morbid exercise, but a path to a more just, clearer, and fuller life.
To remember that we will die is to remember to live.
This awareness can even soothe us, rather than distress us.
Accepting our finitude, ceasing to flee or deny it, is making peace with the condition that is ours.
Those who have faced death often testify to a new serenity, a capacity to savor life that they did not have before.
Not because they fear nothing anymore, but because having accepted the end, they are finally free to fully live the time that remains.
The acceptance of death can be the condition for a truly vibrant life.
Thus ends this long journey, on the highest of questions.
Living knowing that we will die is not a curse to be avoided, but perhaps the very foundation of a conscious and fulfilling life.
This awareness invites us not to postpone the essential, to cherish what is, to give meaning and depth to our counted days.
It reminds anyone learning a language, as well as anyone else, that time is precious, that nothing is guaranteed, and that it is worth living each day as if it mattered — for, in truth, it does.
This is perhaps the oldest and simplest of wisdoms: since life is brief, it is all the more important to live it well.

sentences: At the end of this reflection on our relationship with the living world, a reformulation may be necessary.
We talk about 'protecting nature' as if it were about defending an external reality, an object distinct from us.
But we have seen that this separation between man and nature is misleading, that we are part of the living world, and that our fate is linked to its.

Therefore, the question may not be so much about protecting a nature of which we would be external guardians, but about learning to inhabit the world that is ours — the only one we have, the one from which we both originate and for which we are responsible.

To inhabit is not just to occupy a place, to use it, to exploit it; it is to dwell there, to take care of it, to inscribe oneself in the duration, to feel at home while respecting what precedes and transcends us.
The one who truly inhabits a place does not treat it as a resource to be exhausted, but as a home to be maintained, to which he is connected, belonging to it as much as it belongs to him.
Moving from the idea of protecting nature to that of inhabiting the Earth is a shift from an external relationship to one of belonging, from a logic of management to a logic of care.
This shift has profound consequences.

If we only 'protect nature', we remain in a position of superiority, where man, from the outside, decides to preserve or exploit an object that is foreign to him; nature remains a thing before us, which we manage according to our interests.
If we learn to 'inhabit the Earth', we recognize ourselves as part of a common world, of which we are dependent and responsible, not from above but from within.
The destruction of the living world is no longer the degradation of an external object, but an assault on our own home, on what sustains us and constitutes us.
One does not ravage the house one inhabits.
This way of inhabiting implies a transformation of our relationship with things and beings.
To inhabit is to establish connections, not only of use but of attachment, knowledge, and care, with the places, the living beings, and the balances that surround us.
It is to know one's environment, to become attached to it, to take care of it as something that matters for itself and not just for the use we make of it.

This disposition, which ancient societies often cultivated in their relationship with their territory, has been lost in a world that treats space as a mere support for activities, interchangeable and exploitable.
Relearning it would mean regaining a relationship with the world that is deeper than mere exploitation.
It is not about falling into a mysticism of the Earth, nor about renouncing any transformation of the world, because to inhabit also means to transform, cultivate, and build.
Man cannot inhabit without acting on his environment, and it would be absurd to dream of a human presence without effect.

The difference is not between transforming and not transforming, but between two ways of transforming: one that exhausts and destroys, treating the world as a reserve to be plundered, and one that maintains and cultivates, transforming the world while caring for its sustainability.
To inhabit is to transform while remaining, to act while preserving the conditions of life, to build without destroying what makes building possible.
Learning to inhabit the Earth may be the most accurate name for the ecological task.
Not to protect an external nature in the name of an imaginary purity, nor to manage resources in our best interests, but to relearn to dwell in our world as in a home of which we are part.
This task is more demanding than simple management, as it engages our way of being in the world, our relationship with things and living beings, our conception of our place.

But it is also more fruitful, as it does not only ask us to save a threatened object; it invites us to regain a relationship with the world where we would finally feel at home, not as masters who exploit, but as inhabitants who take care of the only home we have.

sentences: People often contrast the believer and the non-believer as two opposing figures: one would adhere to what cannot be demonstrated, while the other would stick to rational knowledge alone.
This convenient opposition is more complicated than it seems.
For the question of God, the afterlife, and ultimate meaning concerns what, by its nature, eludes demonstration: one cannot prove or refute the existence of God using reason alone.
Thus, believers and non-believers find themselves, in this regard, in a situation closer than they admit: both take a stance on the undemonstrable, and both make a wager in their own way.
Let’s first consider the believer's situation.
His faith is not knowledge: if he is clear-headed, he does not claim to demonstrate what he believes; he adheres to what goes beyond proof, through an act that engages more than reason.
This adherence is not necessarily unreasonable — it can be based on experience, tradition, or reasons to believe — but it involves a part of wager, leap, and trust in what cannot be proven.

The honest believer acknowledges this: his faith is faith, not knowledge, and it retains within it a part of uncertainty and risk, which dogmatic certainty would like to conceal but which true faith embraces.
Now let’s consider the non-believer.
He is often imagined as being solely on the side of knowledge, sticking to the facts, refusing anything that cannot be demonstrated.
However, his position, upon examination, also involves a part of wager.
To assert that there is no God, no afterlife, no ultimate meaning is not a demonstrated knowledge; it is a position on the undemonstrable, just like faith.
The atheist who categorically asserts the non-existence of God also makes a negative act of faith, an adherence to what he cannot prove.
Only the agnostic, who suspends judgment, seemingly escapes the wager — but suspending judgment is still a position, which has its discomfort and its cost.
This symmetry does not mean that all positions are equal, nor that believing and not believing amount to the same thing.
There are reasons to lean one way or the other, arguments to weigh, experiences to consider; the wager is not blind, it can be more or less thoughtful, more or less honest.

Recognizing that both believers and non-believers take a stance on the undemonstrable does not lead to relativism, but to humility: no one holds a certainty on these ultimate questions that would allow them to despise the other.
The believer does not know more than he appears to; the non-believer does not know less than he believes.
This shared humility should transform the relationship between believers and non-believers.
Too often, each treats the other with a contempt that assumes one possesses the obvious truth: the believer pitying the non-believer's blindness, the non-believer mocking the believer's credulity.
However, if all take a stance on the undemonstrable, this mutual contempt is unfounded.
The clear-headed believer knows that his faith is a wager; the clear-headed non-believer knows that his disbelief is one too.

This shared awareness of ultimate uncertainty should establish, between them, not contempt, but respect: that of beings who, faced with the same mystery, have made different wagers, without anyone being able to prove they are right.
Believing and not believing are therefore not opposing positions of knowledge and ignorance, but two ways of positioning oneself in relation to what exceeds knowledge.
This recognition neither weakens faith nor disbelief; it makes them more honest by freeing them from the pretense of a certainty that neither can legitimately claim.
It invites everyone to hold their position with conviction, but without arrogance; to embrace their wager while respecting the one who has wagered differently.

In the face of the ultimate mystery, true wisdom may not lie in the certainty of the dogmatic believer or that of the militant atheist, but in the lucidity of one who knows they believe, or do not believe, without being able to prove it — and draws from it not pride, but humility.

sentences: "Knowledge makes us free," "knowledge liberates": these phrases, so often repeated, express a deep conviction of modernity, which has made knowledge an instrument of emancipation.
Educating the people, spreading the Enlightenment, disseminating knowledge would be to free men from ignorance, superstition, and servitude.
This conviction is not without foundation, and it has inspired noble struggles.
But it deserves to be examined with nuance, as it contains questionable assumptions: does all knowledge liberate, and what does knowledge really free us from?
Let’s first acknowledge what is true in this statement.
It is undeniable that ignorance is a form of servitude, and knowledge is a liberation.
Those who do not know are at the mercy of those who do know, dependent, manipulable, and unable to judge for themselves.
Knowledge frees us from this dependence: it allows us to understand, to judge, to not be deceived, and to make informed decisions.
The history of emancipation is largely the story of access to knowledge, wrested from the privileged who held the monopoly on it.
In this fundamental sense, knowledge does indeed liberate: it gives individuals the means to achieve autonomy, freeing them from the bondage of ignorance.
However, this general truth needs to be clarified, as not all knowledge liberates equally or in the same way.
We must distinguish between knowledge that emancipates and knowledge that merely informs without liberating.
Knowledge can be purely technical, useful without being liberating; it can even enslave when it is used to serve domination, giving a few power over others.
The knowledge of manipulators, propagandists, and those who exploit the understanding of human mechanisms to dominate better is not liberating; it is an instrument of enslavement.
Knowledge is not liberating in itself; it is so according to its nature and the way it is used.
We must also ask what knowledge liberates us from.
Knowledge liberates us from ignorance, certainly, but ignorance is not always a form of servitude, and knowledge does not always bring the happiness that is attributed to it.
There are forms of knowledge that weigh heavily, that oppress, that deprive us of the happy innocence of ignorance; knowledge can be a burden as much as a liberation.

Those who learn the extent of the world's misfortunes, the precariousness of their existence, and the vastness of what they do not know are not necessarily freer or happier; they carry knowledge that can cause them anxiety.
Knowledge liberates us from the deceptive comfort of ignorance, but this is not always for happiness; sometimes it leads to painful clarity.
This nuance does not lead to praising ignorance, nor to renouncing the emancipatory ideal of knowledge.
It invites a more accurate conception of what truly liberates within knowledge.
It is not the accumulation of knowledge that liberates, but a certain relationship to knowledge: the ability to understand, to judge, and to think for oneself.
Liberating knowledge is not the mass of information, but the formation of a mind capable of organizing, critiquing, and using it autonomously.
One can know a lot and not be free if that knowledge remains inert, imposed, and unmastered; one can know less and be freer if what little one knows is truly contemplated.
It is not the quantity of knowledge that liberates, but the quality of the relationship one maintains with it.
Knowledge does indeed make us free, but only if we understand this statement correctly.
Not all knowledge, nor knowledge as mere accumulation, nor knowledge that would guarantee happiness.
But knowledge that shapes judgment, that enables understanding and decision-making for oneself, that frees from the bondage of ignorance without promising a happiness it cannot provide.
This kind of liberation is real and valuable, but it is also demanding: it requires not knowing a lot, but thinking about what we know; not accumulating, but understanding.
The knowledge that liberates is not a treasure we possess, but a light we learn to use — and this light, while it illuminates, does not always provide warmth.

sentences: A life without examination is not worth living." This saying, spoken by a sage more than two millennia ago, can serve as a concluding remark to this long journey — a conclusion that is also, as it should be, a beginning.

For at the end of all these reflections, of this journey through the highest questions, it is right to return to what underlies them all: the idea that a life deserves to be examined, that human existence calls for reflection, and that thinking about one's life is part of living it fully.
This conviction, which has driven this entire journey, deserves one last examination.
What does it mean to examine one's life?

It is not to constantly observe oneself in a sterile introspection, nor to judge oneself with a morbid guilt; it is to reflect on what one does and why, to question one's values, choices, and way of living, not to go through existence without ever asking what one is seeking and whether one is living as one should.

Examining one's life means refusing to live it out of habit, conformity, or inertia, without ever questioning it; it means bringing the light of reflection to it, asking whether one is going where one wants to go, whether one lives according to what one holds to be true and good.
It is the difference between a life endured, lived without awareness, and a life embraced, reflected upon, of which one is a conscious author.
Why would a life without examination not be worth living?
Not that reflection is everything, nor that one must spend one's life philosophizing instead of living.

But because an unexamined life risks passing by itself: pursuing goals that one has not chosen, adopting values that one has not made one's own, being swept along by the current without ever asking where it leads us.

An unexamined life is a life lived without awareness, where one acts without knowing why, where one follows without having chosen; and such a life, however filled it may be, risks not truly being ours, passing by without our having inhabited it consciously.
Examination is what makes a life a human life, lived with awareness, embraced, reflected upon, rather than an existence endured.
This entire journey has, in a sense, been nothing more than an exercise in this examination.

Reflecting on time, death, love, evil, truth, beauty, justice, and wisdom was not about accumulating abstract knowledge; it was about examining our condition, questioning our existence, and illuminating our way of life.

These reflections were not valuable in themselves, like just another piece of knowledge; they were valuable for the light they could shed on our lives, for the way they could transform, deepen, and make our lives more conscious and just.
To think about these questions was to examine one's life; and this examination, if it has any value, is of the kind that makes existence more worthy of being lived.
But this final word is also a beginning, for the examination of a life is never complete.
We never finish examining our lives, questioning them, reflecting on them; it is a task that lasts as long as existence itself, always to be resumed, never finished.
The questions we have addressed have not received definitive answers, nor could they; they remain open, to be contemplated and explored throughout a lifetime.
This journey does not close anything; it opens up, inviting us to continue, to keep examining, reflecting, and searching.
The end is merely a threshold; what has been started here must continue, not just in books, but in life, which is the true place where existence is examined and reflected upon.
And for those who have traveled this path — from a language learned word by word to these texts that raise the highest questions — there may be an image in this very journey.

For learning a language, like examining one's life, is a task that has no end, always to be deepened, never completed; and both transform the one who engages in them, expanding them, making them broader, more aware, more human.

This reader who, having climbed all the levels, can today read and meditate on these texts in a language that was not their own, has done more than learn a language: they have expanded their world, gained access to other thoughts, to other ways of seeing, and, through them, examined their own life.

May this examination continue, in this conquered language and in all others, in books and in existence: for a life that continues to examine itself, to question itself, to seek, is a life that remains alive, open, on a journey.

And perhaps this is the final word, which is a beginning: that true knowledge is not a destination one reaches, but a path one never ceases to travel — and that a life, like a learning process, is only valuable for this very movement of seeking, understanding, and continuing.

sentences: On Sunday morning, many people go to the neighborhood market.
The market starts early, at eight o'clock, and it ends at one o'clock.
There are a lot of people, especially between ten o'clock and noon.
At the market, there are many stalls.
One vendor sells fruits: apples, pears, oranges, and bananas.
Another vendor sells vegetables: tomatoes, carrots, potatoes, and zucchinis.
The vegetables are fresh and they often come from farms near the city.
There is also a bread stall.
The baker sells baguettes, country bread, and croissants.
In the morning, the smell of warm bread attracts many customers.
People often line up in front of this stall because the croissants are very popular.
A little further on, there is a cheese stand.
The seller offers many different cheeses: goat cheese, camembert, comté, and many others.
He sometimes gives small pieces for customers to taste before they buy.
Customers really enjoy this tasting moment.
The market sellers are often very friendly.
They greet customers with a smile and know their habits well.
A seller recognizes a regular customer and asks him for news about his family.
This simple and warm relationship makes the market pleasant for everyone.
Prices are written on small wooden or cardboard signs.
Customers look at the prices before choosing their products.
Sometimes, at the end of the morning, sellers lower the prices a bit to sell the last products that remain on their stand.
A family is strolling peacefully between the stalls.
The parents are choosing vegetables for Sunday dinner, while their children are curiously looking at the colorful fruits.
A child asks his mother to buy strawberries, and his mother happily agrees.
After shopping, many people stop at a café near the market.
They order a coffee or a hot chocolate and sit on the terrace to rest.
It's a simple, calm, and pleasant moment at the end of a busy morning.
The Sunday market is a true moment of life for the local residents.
Many people meet there every week, chat a bit, and enjoy this friendly atmosphere before going home to prepare lunch.

sentences: As she continually complained about Tostes, Charles imagined that the cause of her illness was some local influence, and, fixating on this idea, he seriously considered moving elsewhere.
From then on, she drank vinegar to lose weight, developed a slight dry cough, and completely lost her appetite.
After turning this way and that, Charles learned that there was a large town named Yonville-l'Abbaye in the Neufchâtel district, whose doctor, a Polish refugee, had just fled the previous week.

So he wrote to the local pharmacist to find out the population size, the distance to the nearest colleague, how much his predecessor earned per year, etc.; and since the responses were satisfactory, he decided to move in the spring if Emma's health did not improve.
One day, while preparing for her departure and tidying up a drawer, she pricked her fingers on something.
It was a wire from her wedding bouquet.
The orange blossoms were yellow with dust, and the satin ribbons, edged with silver, were fraying at the edges.
She threw it into the fire.
It ignited faster than dry straw.
Then it looked like a red bush on the ashes, slowly consuming itself.
She watched it burn.
The little cardboard berries burst, the wires twisted, the trim melted; and the crumpled paper corollas, swaying along the plate like black butterflies, finally flew up the chimney.

sentences: And when he lay down on the ground at night, wrapped in his coat next to his snoring comrades, he thought long and hard about his loved ones left behind and the dangers scattered along his path: if he were killed, what would become of the little ones?
Who would feed and raise them?
At that very moment, they were not wealthy, despite the debts he had incurred when leaving to leave them some money.
And Walter Schnaffs sometimes cried.
At the beginning of battles, he felt such weakness in his legs that he would have collapsed if he hadn't thought that the entire army would pass over his body.
The whistling of the bullets made the hair on his skin stand on end.
For months, he had been living in terror and anxiety.
His army corps was advancing towards Normandy; and one day he was sent out on reconnaissance with a small detachment that was simply supposed to explore a part of the country and then fall back.
Everything seemed calm in the countryside; nothing indicated a prepared resistance.

However, the Prussians were quietly descending into a small valley cut by deep ravines when a violent gunfire suddenly stopped them, knocking down about twenty of their men; and a group of sharpshooters, suddenly emerging from a small wood the size of a hand, charged forward, bayonets fixed.
Walter Schnaffs initially remained motionless, so surprised and distraught that he didn't even think of fleeing.
Then a wild desire to run seized him; but he immediately thought that he ran like a turtle compared to the lean Frenchmen who were bounding in like a herd of goats.

Then, spotting a wide ditch full of underbrush covered with dry leaves six paces in front of him, he jumped in feet first, not even thinking about the depth, like one jumps from a bridge into a river.
He passed through a thick layer of vines and sharp thorns that tore at his face and hands, and he fell heavily, sitting down on a bed of stones.
Immediately lifting his eyes, he saw the sky through the hole he had made.

This revealing hole could betray him, and he crawled cautiously on all fours to the bottom of this rut, under the roof of intertwined branches, moving as quickly as possible, away from the scene of the battle.
Then he stopped and sat down again, crouched like a hare among the tall dry grasses.

sentences: A few moments later, the three travel companions were settled in the projectile, having securely fastened the opening plate from the inside, and the mouth of the Columbiad, completely cleared, opened freely to the sky.
Nicholl, Barbicane, and Michel Ardan were definitively sealed in their metal wagon.

The moon was advancing across a sky of crystal clarity, extinguishing the twinkling lights of the stars in its wake; it was then traversing the constellation of Gemini and was almost halfway between the horizon and the zenith.
Everyone could easily understand that they were aiming ahead of the target, just as a hunter aims ahead of the hare he wants to catch.
A terrifying silence hung over the entire scene.
Not a breath of wind on the earth!
Not a breath in their chests!
Their hearts dared not beat.
All the startled gazes were fixed on the gaping maw of the Columbiad.
Murchison was watching the needle of his chronometer.
There were barely forty seconds left before the moment of departure would sound, and each of those seconds felt like a century.
At the twentieth second, there was a universal tremor, and it occurred to the crowd that the daring travelers locked in the projectile were also counting those dreadful seconds!
Isolated cries escaped: Immediately, Murchison, pressing the switch of the device, restored the current and sent the electric spark to the bottom of the Columbiad.
An appalling, unheard-of, superhuman detonation occurred instantly, unlike anything that could be imagined, neither the flashes of lightning nor the roar of eruptions.
A massive jet of fire erupted from the bowels of the earth like from a crater.
The earth heaved, and only a few people could momentarily glimpse the projectile slicing triumphantly through the air amidst the blazing vapors.

At the moment when the incandescent jet rose to the sky to a prodigious height, this outburst of flames illuminated the entire state of Florida, and for an immeasurable instant, day replaced night over a vast expanse of land.
This immense plume of fire was seen from a hundred miles out at sea in the Gulf as well as in the Atlantic, and more than one ship captain noted the appearance of this gigantic meteor in his logbook.

sentences: But what a detestable maxim it is to believe that one's safety can only be found in the oppression of one's people!

Not educating them, not guiding them towards virtue, never making them love you, pushing them through terror to despair, putting them in the dreadful position of either never being able to breathe freely or shaking off the yoke of your tyrannical domination; is that the true way to rule without trouble?
Is that the true path to glory?
After this speech, Idoménée, persuaded by Mentor, hurried to distribute the vacant lands, to fill them with all the useless artisans, and to execute everything that had been decided.
He reserved only for the masons the lands he had destined for them, which they could only cultivate after finishing their work in the city.
At the same time, the city and the surrounding villages were filled with beautiful youth who had long languished in misery and who had not dared to marry for fear of increasing their woes.
When they saw that Idoménée was taking on feelings of humanity and wanted to be their father, they no longer feared hunger and the other scourges with which heaven afflicts the earth.
All that could be heard were cries of joy, the songs of shepherds and laborers celebrating their weddings.
One would have thought to see the god Pan with a crowd of Satyrs and Fauns mingling among the nymphs, dancing to the sound of the flute in the shade of the woods.
Everything was calm and cheerful; but the joy was moderate, and the pleasures served only to relieve the long labors; they were more vivid and pure because of it.
The elders, astonished to see what they had not dared to hope for after such a long age, wept from an excess of joy mixed with tenderness; they raised their trembling hands to heaven.
'Bless, they said, oh great Jupiter, the king who resembles you, and who is the greatest gift you have given us.
He was born for the good of mankind; grant him all the blessings we receive from him.
Our descendants, born from these marriages he favors, will owe him everything, even their birth; and he will truly be the father of all his subjects.
The young men and young women they married only expressed their joy by singing the praises of the one from whom this sweet joy had come.
Their mouths, and even more their hearts, were constantly filled with his name.
They felt happy to see him; they feared losing him: his loss would have been the desolation of every family.

sentences: Oh!
My God, yes.
I seem to be quite uninterested, don't I?
But I assure you it's not my fault that I've taken so long; it will happen one day or another!
I still don't know; it depends on circumstances subject to uncertain combinations.
I wish I could be there when you come; I would try to return, as far as it is in my power, the hospitality you so generously offer me at Monte-Cristo.

I would gladly accept your offer, the host replied; but unfortunately, if I go, it might be incognito. However, the dinner was progressing and seemed to have been served solely for Franz, as the unknown had barely touched one or two dishes of the splendid feast he had offered him, to which his unexpected guest had paid such great honor.
Finally, Ali brought the dessert, or rather took the baskets from the hands of the statues and placed them on the table.
Between the two baskets, he placed a small cup of vermeil closed with a lid of the same metal.
The respect with which Ali had brought this cup piqued Franz's curiosity.
He lifted the lid and saw a kind of green paste that resembled angelica jam, but which was completely unknown to him.
He replaced the lid, just as ignorant of what the cup contained after putting the lid back on as he had been before lifting it, and, looking back at his host, he saw him smile at his disappointment.
"You can't guess, he said to him, what kind of edible this little vase contains, and it intrigues you, doesn't it?"
"Well, this kind of green jam is nothing less than the ambrosia that Hebe served at Jupiter's table."

"But this ambrosia, said Franz, has undoubtedly lost its celestial name in passing through human hands to take on a human name; in common language, what is this ingredient called, for which, by the way, I don't feel much sympathy?"
Ah!

This is precisely what reveals our material origin, exclaimed Sinbad; often we pass by happiness without seeing it, without looking at it, or, if we have seen and looked at it, without recognizing it.
Are you a practical man and is gold your god? Taste this, and the mines of Peru, Guzarat, and Golconda will be opened to you.

Are you an imaginative man, are you a poet? Taste this again, and the barriers of the possible will disappear; the fields of infinity will open up, and you will stroll, free of heart, free of mind, in the boundless realm of daydreaming.

Are you ambitious, do you chase after the greatness of the earth? Always taste this, and in an hour you will be king, not just king of a small kingdom hidden in a corner of Europe, like France, Spain, or England, but king of the world, king of the universe, king of creation.

Your throne will be set on the mountain where Satan took Jesus; and, without needing to pay homage to him, without being forced to kiss his claw, you will be the sovereign master of all the kingdoms of the earth.
Isn't it tempting, what I'm offering you here, and isn't it something very easy since there's nothing else to do?
Look.

Maston was on the verge of going mad, and there were concerns for the brain of this worthy man, who had been so well preserved until then under his gutta-percha skull.
But on the 11th, one of those dreadful storms from the intertropical regions broke out in the atmosphere.
Strong east winds swept away the clouds that had been gathering for so long, and in the evening, the half-eaten disk of the night star majestically passed among the clear constellations of the sky.

That very night, the thrilling news that had been so eagerly awaited burst like a clap of thunder across the States of the Union, and from there, leaping across the Ocean, it raced along all the telegraph wires of the globe.
The projectile had been sighted, thanks to the gigantic reflector at Long's Peak.
Here is the note drafted by the director of the Cambridge Observatory.
It contains the scientific conclusion of this great experiment by the Gun Club.
This projectile did not reach its target.
It passed by, but close enough, however, to be captured by the lunar attraction.
There, its straight-line motion changed into a circular motion of dizzying speed, and it was drawn into an elliptical orbit around the Moon, of which it became the true satellite.
The elements of this new celestial body have not yet been determined.
Neither its translational speed nor its rotational speed is known.
The distance separating it from the surface of the Moon can be estimated at about two thousand eight hundred thirty-three miles (approximately 4,500 leagues).

Now, two hypotheses may arise and lead to a change in the state of affairs: either the attraction of the Moon will ultimately prevail, and the travelers will reach their destination; or, maintained in an immutable order, the projectile will orbit around the lunar disk until the end of time.
What questions this unexpected outcome raised!
What a situation full of mysteries the future held for scientific investigations!
Thanks to the courage and dedication of three men, this seemingly futile endeavor of sending a projectile to the Moon had just yielded an immense result, with incalculable consequences.

The travelers, imprisoned in a new satellite, if they had not reached their goal, were at least part of the lunar world; they were orbiting around the night star, and for the first time, the eye could penetrate all its mysteries.

The names of Nicholl, Barbicane, and Michel Ardan will therefore be forever famous in the annals of astronomy, for these bold explorers, eager to expand the circle of human knowledge, boldly launched themselves through space and risked their lives in the strangest attempt of modern times.
